prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ORACLE CORP" (ticker ORCL), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ORCL", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Oracle Corporation
markets: Cloud business applications (ERP, HCM, SCM - Fusion, NetSuite)
Industry software (hospitality, retail, financial services, construction)

mission.statement: Our mission is to help people see data in new ways, discover insights, unlock endless possibilities.
mission.plain: Oracle wants to help organizations store and use their data so they can make better decisions.

about.plain: Oracle makes the software that big companies and governments use to store and organize huge amounts of information, like bank accounts, orders and patient records. It also rents out giant data centers full of computers, and lately it is building some of the world's biggest AI data centers for companies like OpenAI. And it sells online programs that run a company's accounting, hiring and supply chains.
about.customers: Large companies, governments, hospitals and AI labs around the world buy from Oracle.
about.everyday: When you use a bank card, book a hotel or see a doctor, there is a good chance the records are kept in an Oracle database.

money.plain: rented data-center computers and AI chips
yearly fees to update and support its database and business software
online accounting, HR and supply-chain software (Fusion, NetSuite)
consulting and help setting up systems
one-time sales of database and app software
giant AI training data centers for OpenAI, Meta and others under multi-year contracts

result.summary: Oracle has a durable moat in its database and mission-critical applications because switching away is costly and risky, which supports high-margin support revenue for decades. Its newer AI cloud business is growing explosively (OCI revenue up 121% to $7.4B in Q1 FY2027, $664B of remaining performance obligations) but is capital-intensive, debt-funded and concentrated in a few customers, so its advantage there is less proven.

pricingPower.evidence: Oracle has long charged ~22% of license price per year for support with very high renewal rates, keeping software support revenue near $19.8B in FY2026 even as license sales fell; but in cloud infrastructure it competes on price (OCI markets lower compute and egress prices than AWS) and big AI customers negotiate hard.

moats.evidence: The Oracle Database brand is synonymous with mission-critical reliability among CIOs, but Oracle is not loved by customers and the brand carries little consumer value.

Banks, telecoms and governments run core systems on Oracle Database and E-Business/Fusion apps built over decades; migrating is multi-year and risky, which keeps software support revenue around $19.5-19.8B per year (FY2025-FY2026).
A large pool of Oracle-trained DBAs and partners reinforces adoption, but the products do not get much better for each user as more users join.
OCI's flat network design and lower pricing let it win price-sensitive AI training work, and FY2026 capex of $55.7B buys scale, but AWS, Microsoft and Google spend far more.
Gigawatt-scale AI data centers need power, land and capital few can assemble, but several hyperscalers and neoclouds are all building them.

Oracle runs its database inside AWS, Azure and Google Cloud (Database@AWS/Azure/Google) and offers sovereign/dedicated regions on customer premises, something rivals protecting their own databases are reluctant to copy.
Decades of database engineering (Exadata, Real Application Clusters, Autonomous Database) and fast build-out of large GPU clusters for OpenAI and others are hard to replicate quickly.
Large multi-year AI contracts (e.g., OpenAI's Stargate sites) and secured power sites are valuable but not exclusive; Larry Ellison's influence is a unique but aging asset.

customers.evidence: Retention is very high because systems are hard to replace (support revenue stable at ~$19.8B in FY2026), and RPO jumped to $664B by August 2026, but Oracle is known for aggressive licence audits and is often rated poorly for customer friendliness, so loyalty rests more on lock-in than satisfaction.

talent.evidence: Oracle pays competitively and attracts strong cloud engineers to OCI, but it cut about 21,000 jobs in FY2026 (to ~141,000 staff) and is not usually ranked among the most desirable tech employers.

product.evidence: Oracle Database remains the leading high-end transactional database and Fusion Cloud ERP is a leader in Gartner's cloud ERP rankings; OCI has won AI training work from OpenAI, Meta and others, though AWS and Azure have broader cloud ecosystems.

competitors.name: Amazon (AWS)
competitors.note: Cloud infrastructure and AI compute; Aurora/RDS and Redshift compete with Oracle Database

competitors.name: Microsoft (Azure, Dynamics, SQL Server)
competitors.note: Azure cloud and AI compute, SQL Server database, Dynamics 365 ERP/CRM

competitors.name: Alphabet (Google Cloud)
competitors.note: Cloud infrastructure, AI compute and databases (Spanner, AlloyDB, BigQuery)

competitors.name: SAP
competitors.note: ERP, HCM and supply-chain applications for large enterprises

competitors.name: CoreWeave
competitors.note: GPU cloud / AI training capacity for AI labs (also serves OpenAI and Microsoft)

competitors.name: Salesforce
competitors.note: CRM, customer experience and data cloud applications

competitors.name: IBM
competitors.note: Db2 database, hybrid cloud, consulting and mainframes

competitors.name: Databricks
competitors.note: Data lakehouse, analytics and AI data platform

competitors.name: ServiceNow
competitors.note: Enterprise workflow, IT and HR service management

competitors.name: Epic Systems
competitors.note: Electronic health records, versus Oracle Health (Cerner)

competitors.name: Alibaba Cloud
competitors.note: Cloud infrastructure and databases in Asia

threats: Customer concentration: much of the $664B RPO is tied to a few AI labs (notably OpenAI), whose ability to pay depends on their own fundraising
Debt-funded build-out: notes payable reached about $125B in Aug 2026 and FY2026 free cash flow was -$23.7B
Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google) and neoclouds (CoreWeave, Nebius) competing for the same AI workloads, plus custom chips lowering rivals' costs
Open-source and cloud-native databases (PostgreSQL, Aurora, Snowflake, Databricks) eroding new Oracle Database deployments
Declining license and on-premise software revenue (software revenue -3% in Q1 FY2027) as customers move to SaaS rivals like SAP and Workday
Execution risk on data-center power, construction and GPU supply; key-person risk around 82-year-old chairman Larry Ellison

ceo.name: Clay Magouyrk and Mike Sicilia (co-CEOs)
ceo.background: Magouyrk: software engineer who worked on AWS EC2 before joining Oracle in 2014 to build OCI; Sicilia: led Oracle Industries, joined through Oracle's 2008 acquisition of Primavera. Founder Larry Ellison remains chairman and CTO.

c1.evidence: Oracle leads the mature enterprise database market and is a fast-rising challenger in the fast-growing AI cloud market (OCI revenue +121% to $7.39B in Q1 FY2027), but AWS, Microsoft and Google lead cloud infrastructure.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Oracle Database for proven reliability and Exadata performance and OCI for lower-cost, fast AI clusters, but the AI-cloud edge is mostly price and speed of build, which rivals can copy.

c3.evidence: Oracle is a household name in business and the default for high-end databases, but ordinary consumers rarely use it directly and customers are not known for recommending it enthusiastically.

c4.evidence: Its mission of helping people see data in new ways is generic, though Larry Ellison speaks often about using AI and data to transform healthcare and government; the culture is known as sales- and profit-driven.

c6.evidence: “database giant, expensive, aggressive, Larry Ellison, AI data centers”: the impression is mixed, respected for technology but criticised for licence audits and pricing.

c7.evidence: Cloud infrastructure spending reached about $143B in Q2 2026 (Synergy) and is riding the AI build-out; Oracle targets $225B of revenue by FY2030 versus $67.4B in FY2026.

c8.evidence: Oracle is expanding from databases into AI training/inference clouds, multicloud databases inside AWS, Azure and Google, sovereign clouds, healthcare (Oracle Health) and a stake in the TikTok US joint venture.

m1.evidence: The co-CEOs have a clear plan built on OCI and AI apps, but the long-range vision is still set mainly by chairman and CTO Larry Ellison.

m2.evidence: Neither co-CEO is a founder, but Magouyrk built OCI from scratch at Oracle since 2014 and founder Larry Ellison remains deeply involved as CTO and largest shareholder.

m4.evidence: Oracle's management style is known as hard-driving and top-down, and it cut about 21,000 jobs in FY2026 while spending heavily on data centers.

m5.evidence: OCI under Magouyrk developed a distinctive engineering culture that shipped a competitive cloud from a late start, but Oracle overall is better known for sales than invention.

m6.evidence: Clay Magouyrk is a software engineer who architected OCI's infrastructure, and Larry Ellison as CTO remains hands-on with product.

m7.evidence: There is no clear public record of the co-CEOs' broader purpose; Ellison funds the Ellison Institute of Technology in Oxford, while Oracle itself is seen as profit-focused.

m7b.evidence: No top-university commencement speech by either co-CEO is known; founder Larry Ellison gave the University of Southern California commencement address in 2016.

m8b.evidence: The co-CEOs are low-profile operators; the famous personality at Oracle is founder Larry Ellison.

m9.evidence: Since taking over in Sept 2025, revenue grew 17% in FY2026 to $67.4B and 30% in Q1 FY2027 to $19.3B, with RPO rising to $664B; Magouyrk earlier grew OCI from nothing to a multibillion-dollar business.

m10.evidence: Oracle is not known for frugality; it is spending tens of billions on data centers (FY2026 capex $55.7B) and Ellison is famous for lavish personal spending.

c10.evidence: Oracle software quietly runs banking, telecom, retail, hospital and government systems worldwide, and its AI data centers train widely used models, but it improves lives indirectly rather than as a consumer product.

p2.evidence: Building reliable mission-critical databases and gigawatt-scale AI supercomputers (e.g., the OpenAI Stargate site in Abilene, Texas) is extremely hard and important to the economy.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from FY2021 to FY2026: $40.48B, $42.44B, $49.95B, $52.96B, $57.40B, $67.36B.

f2.evidence: GAAP operating margin fell from 37.6% in FY2021 to 25.7% in FY2022 (Cerner) and recovered to 30.6% in FY2026, still below FY2021; Oracle does not report gross profit.

f3.evidence: At Aug 31, 2026 debt was about $125.3B against $37.1B of cash and investments, though stockholders' equity is positive at $67.2B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $15.21B in FY2021 to $20.61B in FY2026 and operating cash flow from $15.89B to $31.98B, despite a dip in FY2022.

v1.evidence: Oracle Database is widely considered the best for the most demanding transaction systems, but in cloud computing AWS and Azure are seen as the default and OCI mainly wins on price and performance for AI clusters.

v2.evidence: Oracle is not usually ranked among the top tech employers, and it cut about 21,000 jobs (to ~141,000) in FY2026.

c5.evidence: If Oracle disappeared, banks, airlines, hospitals and governments would suffer serious disruption because so many core records run on its databases, and AI labs like OpenAI would lose large amounts of compute, but ordinary people would rarely know the cause.
